# Flexlore guides and templates (full text)

> Practical guides for frontline training from Flexlore (https://www.flexlore.com). English and Turkish.

# Paper vs digital checklists: how to build one your team follows
URL: https://www.flexlore.com/guides/digital-checklists/
Language: en

Use paper checklists when you run one site, the manager reads every sheet and the list rarely changes. Use digital checklists when you need timestamps, photos, one current version and a view across locations. Most operations do best with a hybrid. Either way, a checklist confirms a routine; it does not teach the task.

## What is an operations checklist for?

An operations checklist makes sure a trained person does not skip a step in a routine they already know: opening the kitchen, closing the bar, changing over a line, turning a hotel room. It is a memory aid and a record. It does not teach anyone how to do the task.
Picture a cook opening alone at 6am. The list says "Fryer oil checked and filtered". If she has filtered oil many times, that line keeps her from forgetting it on a busy morning. If she has never done it, the line tells her nothing about how to drain the fryer safely, where the filter paper goes or what tired oil looks like. That knowledge has to come from training, a work instruction or someone showing her.
So a checklist does three jobs well: it keeps a routine the same across shifts and people, it shows the next person what was done, and it gives a manager something to check. It does one job badly: training. For the full difference between the three document types, see SOP vs work instruction vs checklist.

## Paper vs digital checklists: what is the difference?

Paper is fast, cheap and works anywhere, but it is hard to check from another location and easy to fill in after the fact. Digital adds timestamps, photos, a view across locations and one current version, but it depends on a working device and people willing to use it. Neither wins in every case.
 | Paper checklist | Digital checklist | 
Cost to start | Close to nothing: a printer and a clipboard | A device per station or per person, plus the software | 
Speed at the station | A pen tick, no login, no battery | Fast when the device is close and the list is short; slow with wet gloves or a login screen | 
Works without power or signal | Always | Needs a charged device and often a connection | 
Proof of when it was done | A handwritten time, if anyone writes it | A timestamp on each item | 
Photos | No | Yes, for things like a clean fryer or a closed-down line | 
Seeing results from another site | Someone has to collect the sheet or send a picture of it | Same day, by location | 
Changing an item | Reprint and replace every copy; old copies linger | Change once; every location gets the new version | 
Missed items | Visible only when someone reads the sheet | Can be flagged, or required before the list closes | 
Storing records | Binders and boxes; sheets get wet, greasy or lost | Searchable history | 
Typical failure | Everything ticked in one go at the end of the shift | Everything tapped through without looking | 
Look at the last row. Both formats fail the same way: people confirm things they did not check. Changing the format does not fix that. Clear items, and a manager who actually reads the results, do.

## Paper or digital: how do you decide?

Decide by who needs to see the result, how quickly, and how often the list changes. One site with a manager on the floor can run well on paper. Several sites, frequent changes or a need for timed proof usually point to digital, and most operations end up with a mix.
Paper fits when you have one location, the manager sees the sheet every day, the list rarely changes and the station is wet, hot or greasy where a phone does not belong.
Digital fits when you run several locations, head office or an area manager needs to see what happened without calling, items need a photo or a time, or the list changes often enough that old printouts cause mistakes.
A hybrid fits most kitchens, plants and hotels. Keep paper where hands are busy, such as a temperature sheet on the walk-in door, and go digital for the end-of-shift sign-off, the photo of the closed-down line and anything a manager at another site needs. Another common split: paper for the daily routine, digital for weekly deep cleans and internal audits.
Whatever you pick, decide who reviews the results and when. A digital checklist nobody opens is a paper checklist that needs charging.

## How to write checklist items people actually follow

Write each item as one observable action with the standard stated in the line, so anyone can tell whether it is done. "Walk-in at 0 to 4 °C, logged" works. "Check the walk-in" does not, because it never says what good looks like.
One action per item
"Clean and sanitise the slicer and the prep tables" is two or three items, with a chance to skip one each time. Split them.
Make it observable
Someone else should be able to walk up and see whether the item is done. "Hand-wash sink stocked: soap, paper towels, warm water" is observable. "Hygiene OK" is not.
State the standard in the line
Put the number, the setting or the end state where people read it: the temperature, the test strip result, the fill level, the photo it should match. Temperatures in this guide are examples only. Your local food safety rules and your own food safety plan decide the exact limits, so check them before you print anything.
Say what to do when it fails
A reading outside the standard needs a next step, for example "If above the limit, tell the shift lead before using any product". Without one, people tick the box and move on.
Follow the route people walk
Order items the way the person moves through the kitchen, the line or the room, not the order someone thought of them. Backtracking is where items get skipped.
Keep it short
List the things that get missed, or that matter if they are missed. Items everyone does without fail add length and teach people to skim. If one routine needs more than a page, split it by area or by role.

## What goes on a restaurant opening and closing checklist?

An opening checklist confirms the kitchen is safe and ready before the first order: temperatures, hand-wash stations, sanitiser, equipment up to heat, mise en place and dated labels. A closing checklist confirms food is stored, equipment is off and clean, cash is secured and the next shift can open without surprises.
The example below is split into opening and closing, with a standard for every item and columns for time and initials. Adapt it to your menu, your equipment and your local rules. Then walk it with a cook who will use it, in the order they actually move, and cut anything that never gets missed.
Before anyone opens or closes alone for the first time, teach the tasks behind each line. The restaurant onboarding checklist shows where these routines fit in a new hire's first weeks.

## Changeover and room turnover checklist examples

The same rules work outside the kitchen: one action per item, the standard in the line and the order people actually move. Two short examples to adapt.
Manufacturing changeover checklist
Line stopped, lockout applied per site procedure
Previous product, labels and packaging removed from the line
Product contact parts cleaned, no visible residue
Change parts fitted for the new product; settings match the setup sheet
First-piece check passed and signed by the line lead
Lockout removed by the person who applied it; line released
The checklist confirms the changeover happened in full. How to fit each change part belongs in a work instruction or a video, as covered on our manufacturing page.
Hotel room turnover checklist
Linen stripped, bed made to the house standard
Bathroom cleaned and sanitised; towels and amenities set as shown in the standard photo
Minibar checked and restocked, used items recorded
Lost property bagged, labelled and logged
Lights, TV, air conditioning and safe tested
Room marked ready for inspection

## How to roll out a digital checklist across locations

Start with one routine at one or two pilot locations, fix the list with the people who use it, then roll it out with a named owner and a daily review at each site. Moving every checklist to digital on the same day is a reliable way to have none of them used.
Pick one routine. Closing is a good first choice: the result can be checked by the opener next morning.
Pilot it. Run it at one or two sites. Ask staff which items are unclear, slow or pointless, and fix them before anyone else sees the list.
Settle the devices. Decide whether there is a shared tablet at the station or people use their own phones, where it charges and what happens when it is dead. Keep a printed backup.
Name an owner per location. One person checks results every day and follows up on missed or failed items.
Let people see the review. When the area manager comments on last night's closing photos, everyone learns the list is read.
Control versions centrally. One person approves changes, every location gets the same version, and local additions are agreed rather than improvised.
Train the tasks, not only the app. Showing someone where to tap is quick. Showing them how to do each item right is the real work, and it is where on-the-job training comes in.

## Common checklist mistakes

Most checklists fail because they are vague, too long or never reviewed, not because of the format. Watch for these.
Using the checklist to train. A new hire handed the closing list on day one learns what to do, not how to do it.
Vague items. "Clean kitchen", "Check fridges". No standard, no way to verify.
Lists that only grow. Every incident adds a line and nothing is removed. Review the list on a fixed schedule and delete what is never missed.
No response to a failed item. The log shows the walk-in ran warm three nights running and nobody acted. A record without a response protects nobody.
Old versions in use. Last year's sheet is still taped inside a cupboard door. Remove old copies every time the list changes.
Ticks after the fact. Every item signed at the same minute. Ask for times on items where timing matters, and look at them.
Treating the checklist as proof of compliance. A written, dated checklist can support an inspection or audit, but your local rules decide what you must record and keep. Check them.

## Doing this with Flexlore

Flexlore is not a checklist app. It covers the part a checklist cannot: how to do each item right. Film your best person doing the items that take skill, such as filtering fryer oil, probing the walk-in or breaking down the slicer, and mark the steps in the phone editor. AI drafts the instructions and a short quiz, and your team approves them before anything goes out. Keep your checklist on paper or in the tool you already use, and next to each item write the name of its Flexlore job, so anyone unsure can watch it on their phone. You see who watched and passed each job by person and location. Signing someone off on the floor stays with their supervisor. QR codes at the station that open the right job are coming soon.

## Restaurant opening and closing checklist

Restaurant opening and closing checklist

Location: [Location name]
Date: [Date]
Opening lead: [Name]
Closing lead: [Name]
Version: Rev 1, approved by [kitchen manager]

OPENING (before the first order)
#	Item	Standard (what done looks like)	Time	Initials
O1	Walk-in temperature read and logged	0 to 4 °C (example; use your local limit). Above the limit: tell the shift lead before using product		
O2	Reach-in fridges and freezers read and logged	Fridges 0 to 4 °C, freezers -18 °C or colder (examples)		
O3	Hand-wash sinks stocked	Soap, paper towels and warm water at every sink		
O4	Sanitiser made up and tested	Test strip shows the strength on the product label		
O5	Fryer oil checked	Level at the fill line; colour and smell acceptable, or filtered or changed per the oil SOP		
O6	Grill, ovens and fryers on	At set temperature before the first order		
O7	Mise en place checked by station	Matches the prep list; every container labelled and dated		
O8	Use-by dates checked	Anything past date removed and recorded as waste		
O9	Dish machine ready	Filled, chemicals connected, test cycle run		
O10	Front of house ready	Floor clean and dry, tables set, toilets checked and stocked		
O11	Till ready	Float counted and signed		
O12	Pre-shift briefing done	Specials, sold-out items and allergen changes told to the team		

CLOSING (after the last order)
#	Item	Standard (what done looks like)	Time	Initials
C1	All food stored	Covered, labelled and dated; raw below ready-to-eat		
C2	Final fridge and walk-in temperatures logged	Within your limit; doors fully closed		
C3	Fryers off	Oil filtered or covered		
C4	Grill, ovens and burners off	Gas valves closed where your procedure requires		
C5	Surfaces cleaned and sanitised	Prep tables, boards and slicer: no visible residue		
C6	Floors and drains done	Swept, mopped, drain covers cleared		
C7	Bins emptied	New liners in; outside bin lid closed		
C8	Dish machine drained and cleaned	Filters out, rinsed and replaced		
C9	Hand-wash sinks restocked for opening	Soap and paper towels full		
C10	Cash secured	Counted, in the safe, end-of-day report signed		
C11	Building secured	Extraction and lights off, doors locked, alarm set		

Sign-off
Opening lead: [signature]
Closing lead: [signature]
Manager review next day: [signature]
Failed items, action taken and who was told: [notes]

Temperatures are examples. Your local food safety rules and your food safety plan decide the limits.

## Questions

**Is a digital checklist better than a paper one?**
Not always. Digital is better when you need timestamps, photos, one current version and results from several locations without calling. Paper is better at a wet or greasy station, with no battery or login to fail. Many restaurants and plants use both: paper where hands are busy, digital for sign-offs and anything a manager needs to see remotely.

**What should be on a restaurant opening and closing checklist?**
Opening: fridge and walk-in temperatures, hand-wash sinks stocked, sanitiser tested, equipment at temperature, mise en place and date labels checked, and a pre-shift briefing. Closing: food stored and labelled, final temperatures, equipment off and cleaned, floors, drains and bins done, cash secured and the building locked. Adapt the list to your menu and local rules.

**How do I get staff to actually follow a checklist?**
Keep it short, write each item as one observable action with the standard in the line, and order it the way people walk. Then make sure someone reviews the results every day and acts on failed items. Staff follow lists they know are read. Teach the tasks behind the items before handing the list over.

**How long should an operations checklist be?**
As short as it can be while covering what gets missed or matters if missed. If one routine runs over a page, split it by area or by role, such as kitchen closing and front-of-house closing. Remove items that are never missed, because long lists teach people to skim and tick without looking.

**Can a checklist replace training?**
No. A checklist reminds a trained person what to confirm. It does not show how to filter fryer oil, set up a machine or make a bed to the house standard. Teach each task first, with a work instruction, a short video or someone showing it, and use the checklist afterwards to keep the routine consistent.

**Do digital checklists help with food safety inspections?**
A written, dated checklist with times and initials can support an inspection or internal audit, whether it is on paper or digital. Digital records are easier to search and harder to lose. Neither format makes you compliant on its own. Your local food safety rules decide what you must record, how and for how long, so check them.

**How often should I update an operations checklist?**
Review it on a fixed schedule, for example each quarter, and whenever equipment, the menu or the process changes. After any incident, check whether an item was missing or unclear. When you change the list, remove every old copy so only the current version is in use at every location.

# Employee training tracker: a free template, and when to outgrow the spreadsheet
URL: https://www.flexlore.com/guides/employee-training-tracker/
Language: en

Track employee training with one record per person per training: who was trained, on which procedure and version, when, by whom, how it was checked and when the refresher is due. A shared spreadsheet works for a few sites and trainings. Move to software when versions, locations or missed refreshers outgrow it.

## What is an employee training tracker?

An employee training tracker is a log of who was trained on what, when, by whom and how it was checked. It is the record you open when someone asks "has the new cashier done allergen training?" or "who still needs the updated fryer procedure?"
It is not the same as a skills matrix. A training matrix shows coverage: who can run each station on each shift, at what level. A tracker is the history behind it: each training event, dated, with the version of the procedure and the proof. Most teams need both, and the tracker feeds the matrix.
Picture a café with three sites. The owner rewrites the espresso cleaning routine in March. In June, a barista at the second site is still doing it the old way. A good tracker shows that she was trained in January, on version 3, and never saw version 4. Without it, you find out from the machine.

## What should a training record include?

Record one row per person per training, with enough detail that someone who was not there can see what happened. These columns cover it:
Employee, role and location. Role decides which trainings are required. Location lets you filter by site.
Training or SOP name. Use the exact name of the written procedure, picked from a list, so "Allergens" and "Allergen training" do not become two trainings.
Version. The version of the procedure the person learned. This is the column most trackers skip and the one that matters most when a job changes.
Date trained. A real date, not text, so you can calculate from it.
Trained by. The person who showed the job. It tells you who to ask, and who trains well.
Check method. Quiz, observed on shift, or both. A signature on a sheet shows someone attended; it does not show they understood.
Result. Pass, Not yet, or Retrain.
Refresher due. The date the training should be repeated, if the job needs a refresher.
Keep one row per person per training, never one row per person with trainings in columns. When Sam does his fryer refresher, add a new row. The old row stays, so the history stays.

## How to set up a training tracker in Excel or Google Sheets

Use two tabs: a training list that defines each training once, and a records tab that logs every training event. Then let formulas and color do the checking.
Build the training list first. One row per training: name, current version, roles that need it, refresher interval in months, and an owner who keeps the procedure up to date.
Create the records tab. Use the columns from the template above, with headers in row 1. Format it as a table so filters and formulas extend to new rows.
Add data validation. Make Training a dropdown that pulls from the training list. Do the same for Location, Check method (Quiz, Observed, Quiz + observed) and Result (Pass, Not yet, Retrain). Set Date trained to accept dates only.
Calculate the refresher date. Use EDATE on the date trained plus the interval from the training list, so nobody types refresher dates by hand.
Add a Status column. The formula in the template returns Not started, Retake quiz, Retrain: old version, Overdue, Due soon or OK.
Add conditional formatting. Color the row red when Refresher due is before TODAY(), amber when it is within 30 days, and grey when the version is older than the current one.
Freeze and protect. Freeze the header row and the first column. Lock the formula columns and the training list so only the owner can change them.
Enter training on the day it happens. A shift lead who logs sessions on Friday from memory will get dates and names wrong.

## How to report from a training tracker

A tracker is only useful if it answers a few questions quickly. Set up these views once and check them at the same time each week, for example before the rota is published.
What is overdue? Filter Status to Overdue and sort by location. This is the list for each site manager.
Who is on an old version? Filter Status to "Retrain: old version". After any change to a procedure, this list is the follow-up plan.
Completion by location. A pivot table with locations in rows, trainings in columns and a count of Pass shows which site is behind.
Who has not started? This is the hard one. A tracker only holds trainings that happened. To see gaps, you need a roster tab that lists every person and role, then compare it with the trainings each role requires. Many teams add one placeholder row per required training for each new hire, with Status "Not started", as Chris has in the example.
Keep the weekly report short: overdue, old version and not started, per location. A manager can act on three lists. A dashboard with twelve charts usually gets ignored.

## Spreadsheet vs training software: which do you need?

A spreadsheet is enough while one person owns it, there are a handful of trainings and the team works at one or two sites. Software starts to earn its place when the training itself, not just the record, needs to reach people on the floor.
What you need | Spreadsheet | Training software | 
Cost to start | Usually nothing extra | A subscription | 
Setup | An afternoon with the template | Account setup, roles, importing people | 
Recording a training | Someone types each row | Recorded when the person finishes the training or quiz | 
Proof it was understood | Whatever you write in Check method | Quiz results stored with the record | 
Procedure changes | You update the version and find who to retrain | Depends on the tool; check that it can re-assign the new version to the people affected | 
Several locations | Shared file or one copy per site, merged by hand | One system, filtered by location and role | 
Reminders | Conditional formatting you have to open to see | Depends on the tool; check for due-date notifications | 
Who can see and edit | File sharing settings | Roles and permissions by person and site | 
Flexibility | Any column, any format | Limited to what the tool supports | 
Neither option signs someone off on the floor. That stays with the supervisor who watched them work. If you are also weighing what kind of software fits, the guide on LMS vs SOP software compares the two main types.

## Signs you have outgrown the spreadsheet

You have outgrown the spreadsheet when keeping it right takes more time than the training it records. These are the usual signs:
Each site keeps its own copy and nobody is sure which file is current.
Rows are entered days or weeks after the training, from paper sign-in sheets.
You cannot answer "who has not seen the new version?" without an hour of filtering.
The tracker records that training happened, but the training itself lives somewhere else: a binder, a folder of videos, or one experienced person.
Refreshers are missed because nobody opened the file that week.
New hires start faster than anyone can add them to the sheet, as in seasonal hiring.
Frontline staff never see the tracker, so they do not know what they still need to do.
One or two of these can be fixed with better habits. When most of them are true, the problem is the tool, not the people using it.

## How to track training across several locations

Use one tracker with a Location column, not one file per site. Separate files drift apart: different training names, different columns, different ideas of what "Pass" means.
One training list for everyone. Head office or the operations lead owns the names, versions and refresher intervals. Sites add rows to the records tab; they do not invent new trainings.
Location-specific trainings are still on the list. If only the airport site has a certain dish machine, add that training with "Airport" in a Location column on the training list.
A named owner per site. One person at each location enters records and works the weekly overdue list.
Compare sites on the same three numbers. Overdue, old version and not started. Avoid ranking sites on total trainings logged; a site with high turnover will always log more.
People who work at two sites get one row per training, not one per site. Record where they were trained.

## Common training tracker mistakes

No version column. The record says trained, but on a procedure that has since changed.
Attendance as proof. A signature shows presence. Add a quiz or an observation to show understanding.
Free-text training names. Typos split one training into several and break every count.
Overwriting old rows. When a refresher replaces the original date, the history is gone.
Tracking training that does not exist in writing. If there is no written or filmed standard, "trained" means whatever the trainer showed that day. Write the procedure first, then track it.
Logging only classroom sessions. Most frontline learning happens at the station. Record on-the-job training the same way, with the trainer and the check.

## Doing this with Flexlore

Flexlore keeps the training and the record in the same place. Your best person films the job on a phone, marks the steps in the phone editor, and AI drafts the written steps and a short quiz. Your team reviews and approves each draft before it is assigned.
When people watch the job and take the quiz, you see who has watched and who passed, by person, team and location, without anyone typing a row. Roles and workspaces keep each site to its own jobs. When a job changes, you edit the steps and publish the new version. The apps run on iOS and Android, in 8 languages. People get a push when a new job is added. Reminders and a web panel for managers are coming soon. Signing people off on the floor stays with your supervisor. Plans are by number of users; see pricing.

Fryer start-up and oil check	v3	Line cook, Lead cook	6	Head chef

FORMULAS (row 2 of the records tab)
Refresher due (J2)	=IF(F2="","",EDATE(F2,VLOOKUP(D2,'Training list'!A:D,4,FALSE)))
Status (K2)	=IF(F2="","Not started",IF(I2<>"Pass","Retake quiz",IF(E2<>VLOOKUP(D2,'Training list'!A:B,2,FALSE),"Retrain: old version",IF(J2<TODAY(),"Overdue",IF(J2-TODAY()<=30,"Due soon","OK")))))

What this example shows: Sam's fryer refresher is overdue, Jordan was trained on an old allergen version, Elif needs to retake the espresso quiz, and Chris has not started the closing routine.

## Questions

**How do I make a training tracker in Excel?**
Create two tabs. The first lists each training with its current version and refresher interval. The second logs one row per person per training: employee, role, location, training, version, date, trainer, check method, result and refresher due. Use dropdowns for names, EDATE for refresher dates and conditional formatting to turn overdue rows red.

**What is the difference between a training tracker and a training matrix?**
A training tracker is a dated log of each training event: who, what, which version, when and how it was checked. A training matrix is a grid of people and jobs that shows skill levels and coverage per shift. The tracker is the evidence; the matrix is the summary a manager uses to plan shifts and cross-training.

**How often should employees repeat training?**
It depends on the job and on local rules. Set a refresher interval per training on your training list, shorter for safety and hygiene tasks and longer for routine ones, and check what your local regulations or industry standards require. Also retrain whenever the procedure changes, regardless of the interval.

**What should a training record include for an audit?**
At minimum: the person, the training or procedure name and version, the date, who delivered it, how understanding was checked and the result. Keep the written or filmed procedure the record refers to. Auditors and local rules differ, so check what your inspector or standard expects before relying on any template.

**Can Google Sheets work as a training tracker for several locations?**
Yes, for a while. Use one shared file with a Location column, one training list owned by head office and a named person per site who enters records. It starts to strain when sites keep separate copies, records are entered late, or you cannot quickly see who still needs an updated procedure.

**Is a signed attendance sheet enough proof of training?**
It proves someone was present, not that they understood or can do the job. Add a check: a short quiz shows they understood the steps, and a supervisor watching them work on a real shift confirms they can do it. Record which check was used in the tracker.

**When is it worth paying for training tracking software?**
When keeping the spreadsheet right costs more time than it saves: several sites with their own copies, frequent procedure changes, many new hires, or missed refreshers. If the training content also lives in binders or one person's head, software that holds both the training and the record usually solves more than a better sheet.

# LMS vs SOP software: which one does a frontline team need?
URL: https://www.flexlore.com/guides/lms-vs-sop-software/
Language: en

An LMS (learning management system) manages courses: assigning them, tracking completion and certifying people. SOP software manages procedures: how one specific task is done, opened on the job and updated when the task changes. Desk-based teams with long compliance courses usually need an LMS; frontline teams learning hands-on tasks usually need SOP software first.

## What is the difference between an LMS and SOP software?

An LMS is built around courses. SOP software is built around tasks. That one difference shapes everything else: how content is made, where people open it, and how you know someone is ready.

A traditional LMS (learning management system) is designed to deliver structured learning. You build or buy a course, assign it to a group, people complete modules in order, and the system records scores, completion dates and certificates. It answers the question &quot;has this person completed the required training?&quot;

SOP software is designed to hold the way work is done. Each item is one procedure, such as closing the fryer station, changing over line 2 or turning a hotel room. People open it at the moment they need it, often on a phone, and the procedure is updated when the task changes. It answers the question &quot;does this person know how we do this job here, today?&quot;

The third option most teams already have is a shared drive or documents: Word files, PDFs, printed binders and photos in a group chat. It costs nothing extra, but nobody can tell which version is current or who has read it.

## LMS vs SOP software vs shared drive: side by side

Each category is good at different things. Use the table to see which column matches the work your people actually do.

Question | Traditional LMS | SOP software | Shared drive / documents | 

Main unit of content | Course or module, often with several lessons | One procedure for one task | A file | 

Typical length | Minutes to hours per course | A few short steps | Anything from one page to a full manual | 

Who usually creates content | Training team, instructional designers or bought-in course libraries | The people who do the job, approved by their manager | Whoever has time | 

Where it is used | Mostly at a desk or in a training room | At the station, on a phone, during the shift | At a desk, or printed at the station | 

When it is used | Scheduled training time, onboarding week, annual refreshers | Before and during the task, and whenever someone forgets a step | When someone remembers it exists | 

How understanding is checked | Graded assessments, exams, certificates | A short quiz per procedure, plus a supervisor sign-off on the floor | Usually not checked | 

How updates reach people | Course revision, often a larger project | Change one step, approve, publish the new version | New file, old copies keep circulating | 

What managers see | Completion and scores by course and learner | Who learned each task, by person, team and location | Nothing reliable | 

Strongest fit | Compliance courses, certification tracking, office and knowledge roles | Hands-on tasks, high turnover, many locations, shift work | Very small teams with few tasks | 

Neither software column is better in general. They solve different problems, and the right choice depends on what you are trying to fix.

## When is an LMS the right tool?

An LMS is the right tool when the training is a course: structured, sequential, and the same for everyone in a role. It is genuinely strong in several areas.

Long compliance and policy courses. Topics like anti-harassment, data protection or code of conduct are taught as courses with a final assessment. An LMS is designed for exactly this.

Certification tracking. If people hold certificates that expire and must be renewed, an LMS can track expiry dates and assign refreshers.

Desk-based staff. Office, sales, support and management roles sit at computers, have scheduled learning time and can work through modules.

Bought-in content libraries. Generic skills such as leadership, software training or communication are often available as ready-made courses that run in an LMS.

Learning paths and career development. Multi-course programs for supervisors or future managers fit the course-and-path model well.

If most of your training need looks like this list, an LMS is probably your main system, and procedures may only be a small addition.

## Why do frontline teams often need something different?

Frontline work is learned by doing, at the station, during a shift. The course format was not designed around that setting, so the fit is often weaker even when the LMS itself is good.

Picture a new hire on the fryer at 7am. They do not need a long slide module on kitchen safety. They need to see how oil is checked and filtered on this fryer, in this kitchen, in five short steps, and to replay step 3 when they forget it on Thursday.

Common friction points when a course-first approach meets frontline work:

No desk, no scheduled learning time. People learn between tasks, on their own phone, often in noise or with gloves on.

Content comes from the floor. The best operator or chef knows the job. Turning that into a formal course usually needs a training team in the middle.

Tasks change often. A new menu item, a new machine setting or a new cleaning product means one step changes. Updating a procedure is quick; revising a course is usually a bigger job.

Completion is not the same as readiness. Finishing a module shows someone sat through it. A manager wants to know who can run the dish machine on Saturday.

This is where short, task-sized content works better. Our guide to microlearning for frontline workers covers why short steps stick and how to write them.

## Do I need an LMS, SOP software, or both? A decision checklist

Start from the problem you want to fix, not the software category. Use the table first, then answer the checklist questions.

Choose an LMS when... | Choose SOP software when... | Use both when... | 

Most of your staff work at desks and have scheduled learning time | Most of your staff work on the floor, on shifts, without a computer | You have a large office or head office team and a large frontline team | 

Your main need is long compliance or policy courses | Your main need is showing how specific tasks are done the same way everywhere | You must deliver formal courses and also standardize daily tasks | 

You must track certificates and renewal dates | You need to see who learned each task, by person and location | Certificates live in one system, task readiness in the other | 

Content is built by a training team or bought as a library | Content should come from the people who do the job best | The training team owns courses; operations owns procedures | 

Content changes once or twice a year | Tasks, recipes, machines or standards change every few weeks | Policies change slowly, but the work on the floor changes often | 

Then answer these questions honestly. Each &quot;yes&quot; points toward SOP software.

Do new hires mainly learn by shadowing someone, with results that depend on who they shadow?

Do two locations do the same task differently?

Are the printed procedures at the station older than the equipment?

Would your staff open training on a phone during a shift rather than at a computer?

Is there one experienced person who is the only one who really knows a job?

When a step changes, do you struggle to know who has seen the change?

And these point toward an LMS:

Do you have mandatory courses with formal assessments that must be repeated on a schedule?

Do you need to manage certificates with expiry dates?

Do you want to buy ready-made courses on general topics rather than create your own?

Many &quot;yes&quot; answers in both lists usually means you need both. If you answered &quot;no&quot; to almost everything, a clear folder structure and a solid SOP template may be enough for now. When you are ready to compare tools, our guide to choosing SOP software has a scoring checklist and demo questions.

## How do you use an LMS and SOP software together?

Split the work by content type: courses in the LMS, task procedures in SOP software. Then agree who owns each and where managers look for readiness.

A simple split

LMS: company induction, policies, compliance courses, certifications with renewal dates, leadership and office skills.

SOP software: opening and closing routines, recipes, cleaning, machine start-up and changeovers, room standards, anything done with the hands at a station.

Rules that keep it clean

One home per piece of content. Do not keep the same procedure in both places. If a course needs a task, it points to the procedure instead of copying it.

Clear owners. The training or HR team usually owns courses. Operations, a head chef or a production lead usually owns procedures and approves changes.

One readiness view per question. &quot;Who is certified?&quot; is answered in the LMS. &quot;Who can run this task on Saturday?&quot; is answered in SOP software, with the supervisor's sign-off on the floor.

Onboarding uses both. Day 1 may be policy courses; days 2 to 10 are the tasks for the role, learned at the station with a supervisor nearby.

If you only track all of this in a spreadsheet today, our employee training tracker guide shows how to lay out people, tasks and sign-offs in one view.

## What changes for restaurants, manufacturing, hotels and franchises?

The decision logic stays the same; the balance between courses and procedures shifts with the work.

Restaurants and cafés: most learning is task-based (recipes, plating, opening and closing, cleaning, allergen steps) and turnover is often high. SOP software usually carries the daily load. Formal food safety training may still be delivered as a course or by an external provider, depending on local rules.

Manufacturing: changeovers, machine start-up, PPE and lockout steps are task procedures and benefit from close-up video and strict approvals. Formal safety certificates and periodic refresher courses often fit an LMS. Many plants need both, plus a supervisor sign-off before someone runs a machine alone.

Hotels: housekeeping room turns and front desk check-in are visual, standard-driven tasks that suit procedures. Guest service, brand values and policy training are often delivered as courses.

Franchises: head office needs to launch a new menu item or process once and see completion by location. Procedures with readiness by location answer that directly. Franchisee onboarding and brand policies may still run as courses.

Whatever the industry, a large part of frontline learning still happens next to an experienced colleague. Our on-the-job training guide shows how to structure that so procedures and supervisor sign-off work together.

## Doing this with Flexlore

Flexlore is SOP software for frontline teams, not an LMS. Available now: film a job on a phone, split it into steps in the phone editor, and let AI draft the instructions and a short quiz that your team edits and approves. Assign by role and location, and see completion and quiz results by person, team and location. iOS and Android apps, with the app in 8 languages. A quiz shows who understood the steps; signing someone off on the floor stays with their supervisor.

Coming soon: PDF to steps, screen recording, automatic translation, QR codes on the job, reminders, a web panel for managers, and AI agents and MCP.

If you already run an LMS, Flexlore can sit beside it for the hands-on tasks. Plans are by number of users; see pricing, or book a demo and build one of your own tasks with us.

## Questions

**Can SOP software replace an LMS?**
For some frontline teams, yes, if their training is almost all hands-on tasks and they have no formal certification needs. If you must deliver long compliance courses, manage certificates with expiry dates or train large office teams, an LMS still does that job better. Many organizations use SOP software for tasks and an LMS for courses.

**Is an LMS a good fit for frontline workers?**
It can be, for courses such as policies, compliance and certifications. It is a weaker fit for learning daily tasks at the station, because courses are built for scheduled learning time, often at a desk. Frontline staff usually need short, task-sized steps on a phone they can replay during a shift.

**What is the difference between SOP software and a knowledge base?**
A knowledge base stores articles people can search. SOP software adds what a manager needs for procedures: approval before anything goes live, version control, assignment by role and location, a check for understanding, and a view of who has learned each task. A knowledge base answers questions; SOP software also tracks readiness.

**Do small businesses need an LMS?**
Usually not at first. A small restaurant, café or workshop mostly needs its daily tasks written or filmed clearly and a way to see who has learned them. An LMS starts to make sense when you have formal courses to deliver, certificates to track or a growing office team with scheduled learning time.

**Can we use our existing PDFs and documents?**
Yes, as a starting point. Existing documents show what the standard should be. For frontline tasks, the usual next step is to break each document into short steps and add video where seeing the task matters. Review every document with the person who does the job today, because written procedures often drift from real practice.

**How do I track training if we use both an LMS and SOP software?**
Decide which system answers which question. Course completion and certificates are tracked in the LMS. Task readiness, meaning who has learned each procedure and passed its quiz, is tracked in SOP software, with the supervisor's sign-off on the floor. Keep one owner for each and avoid copying the same content into both.

**Does an LMS or SOP software make us compliant?**
No software makes you compliant by itself. Local rules decide which training, procedures and records you need, so check them with your authority or advisor. Clear, approved procedures and records of who was trained can support an audit, but inspectors look at what actually happens on the floor.

# Microlearning vs classroom training for shift workers
URL: https://www.flexlore.com/guides/microlearning-for-frontline-workers/
Language: en

Microlearning is training delivered in short, focused lessons, each teaching one task or one idea that a person can finish in a few minutes, often on a phone. For shift workers it usually means one short video of one job, split into a few steps, followed by a quick quiz and watched close to when the task is done.

## What is microlearning?

Microlearning is training split into short lessons, each covering one task or one idea, that people can finish in a few minutes. Instead of a half-day course on &quot;kitchen closing&quot;, a cook gets one lesson on closing the fryer, another on cleaning the flat top and another on labeling and storing prep.

For frontline and shift teams, a good micro lesson has four parts:

One task. Something a person does with their hands at a station, from start to finish.

One short video. The task filmed where it happens, by the person who does it best.

A few steps. The video cut into steps with a line of text each, so people can replay only the part they need.

A short quiz. A handful of questions about the decisions that matter, to show who understood.

The format fits shift work because it matches how the work is organized. People start at different times, rarely sit together in one room, and learn a station at a time. A lesson they can watch on their own phone before a shift, or at the station right before the task, works with that schedule instead of against it. If you are new to filming jobs, our guide on how to make a video SOP covers the basics.

## Microlearning vs classroom training: which is better?

Neither is better on its own. Classroom training is the right tool for culture, group practice and topics that need discussion. Microlearning is the right tool for single tasks, refreshers and teams that never sit in one room at the same time. Most teams need both.

Question | Microlearning | Classroom training | 

Best for | One task at a time: a machine setting, a cleaning routine, a station closing | Culture, values, service style, topics that need questions and discussion | 

Hands-on practice | Shows the task; practice still happens at the station with a supervisor | Group practice with a trainer watching, role play, drills | 

Complex topics | Weak on its own; works as the reference after the session | Strong: a trainer can explain, answer and adjust | 

Shift schedules | Fits any shift; each person watches when they can | Hard to gather night, weekend and part-time staff together | 

Refreshers | Easy to rewatch one step before doing the task | Rarely repeated; people forget between sessions | 

Consistency across locations | Every location sees the same lesson | Depends on who runs the session at each site | 

Updating | Replace the one lesson or step that changed | Update the slides and retrain everyone in a new session | 

Team connection | Low; people learn alone | High; new hires meet each other and the managers | 

A simple rule: if the goal is for someone to do one thing correctly, a micro lesson plus practice is usually enough. If the goal is for a group to understand, agree or feel part of the team, bring them together.

## When should you not use microlearning?

Do not use microlearning for topics that need judgment built through conversation, for skills that need supervised practice before anyone is safe, or as a way to skip the first day of welcome. Short lessons support these, but they do not replace them.

Culture and welcome. A new hire&#39;s first hours should include a real person showing them around, introducing the team and explaining how things work here.

High-risk tasks. Forklift driving, lockout on a large machine, handling hazardous chemicals. A video can prepare someone, but supervised practice and a formal sign-off come first. Local rules may also require a specific course, so check them.

Complex judgment. Handling an angry guest, deciding when to stop a line, managing a team. These need discussion, examples and feedback from someone experienced.

Long connected processes. Cutting a full process into pieces can hide how the pieces fit. Give the big picture first, then the micro lessons for each part.

Topics where the answer is &quot;it depends&quot;. If every case is different, a fixed lesson will mislead more than it helps.

## How to create microlearning: turn one job into micro lessons

Pick one task, film it once, cut it into a few steps, add a short quiz, and have it approved. Repeat for the next task. Here is the process in order.

List the tasks in the job. Walk through a shift and write down every task a new person must learn at one station. Each line on that list is a candidate lesson.

Start with the tasks that cause questions. The ones new hires ask about most, or where mistakes are costly. Film those first.

Film one task per video. Film the person who does it best, at the real station, saying what they do and why.

Cut it into a few steps. Each step is one action with one result. If a lesson has many steps, it is probably two tasks.

Write one or two lines per step. Start with a verb. Put exact values, limits and warnings in the text, not only in the speech.

Add a short quiz. A few questions about decisions people get wrong, not trivia.

Have it checked and approved. The expert confirms the steps, the manager who owns the standard approves it.

Assign it by role. A server does not need the dish machine lesson in week one.

## Microlearning examples from the floor

The best examples are tasks with a clear start, a clear end and a right way to do them. Here is one worked through in full, and two shorter ones.

Worked example: closing the fryer

Lesson title: Closing the fryer station. Filmed by the most experienced line cook at the end of a quiet evening.

Turn the fryer off and let the oil cool to the safe level set in your kitchen.

Put on heat-resistant gloves and an apron before touching the drain.

Remove the baskets and place them in the sink for washing.

Filter or drain the oil following your house procedure; check the container is in place first.

Wipe the fryer surfaces and the area around it, then check the floor for spills.

Quiz questions:

What do you check before you open the drain valve?

When is the oil cool enough to drain in this kitchen?

What do you do if oil spills on the floor?

Short example: a machine changeover

On a packaging line, a format change is a series of lessons, not one: stopping and isolating the machine, swapping the change parts, setting the guides, running and checking the first pieces. Each one gets its own video, steps with the exact settings as text, and a few questions on the checks before restart.

Short example: turning down a hotel room

Evening turndown is one lesson: dim the lights, fold back the bed to house standard, place the amenity, close the curtains, tidy the bathroom and leave the room as the guest expects. The quiz asks about the house details people get wrong, such as which side the bed is folded from and what to do if the guest is in the room.

## A blended training plan for a new hire's first two weeks

A blended plan uses classroom or face-to-face time for welcome, culture and supervised practice, and micro lessons for each task as it comes up. Here is an example for a new line cook. Adapt the tasks to your own role.

When | Face to face | Micro lessons | Check | 

Day 1 | Welcome, tour, team introductions, safety and hygiene basics with a manager | Handwashing, uniform and personal hygiene | Manager walks through the kitchen with them | 

Days 2 to 3 | Shadow a trainer at the prep station | Knife safety, labeling and dating prep, cold storage | Quiz on each lesson; trainer watches prep | 

Days 4 to 5 | Work the prep station with the trainer nearby | Opening the line, temperature checks | Supervisor watches one opening | 

Week 2, early | Shadow the fry and grill stations during a quiet service | Fryer use, closing the fryer, cleaning the flat top | Quiz; supervisor watches each task once | 

Week 2, late | Short group session with the head chef on service standards and questions | Allergen steps, plating for the main dishes | Supervisor sign-off on each station | 

End of week 2 | One-to-one review with the manager | Rewatch any lesson with missed quiz questions | Agree what to practice next | 

The micro lessons do not replace the trainer; they mean the trainer spends time on practice and feedback instead of repeating the same explanation. For how the supervised part works, see our guide to on-the-job training.

## Refreshers and spaced repetition, in plain words

People forget what they learned once and never used again. Spaced repetition means bringing the same lesson back a few times, with growing gaps in between, so it sticks. Micro lessons make this practical because each one is short.

Repeat close to use. The best refresher is watching the steps right before doing a task you have not done for a while.

Space it out. Bring a lesson back after a few days, then after a few weeks, instead of repeating it many times in one sitting.

Use the quiz as the refresher. Answering the questions again is a quick way to check what has faded.

Refresh rare tasks on purpose. Deep cleaning, a rare changeover, an emergency procedure. These are the ones people forget first.

Refresh after changes. When a recipe, setting or rule changes, send the updated lesson to everyone who learned the old one.

For more on why one-time onboarding fades, read why one-time onboarding does not hold.

## How do you know if microlearning is working?

Look at three things together: who completed each lesson, how they did on the quiz, and what supervisors see on the floor. Any one of them alone can mislead.

Completion. Who has watched each lesson assigned to them, by person, team and location. Gaps show who has not been trained yet, not who is failing.

Quiz results. Which questions people miss. If many people miss the same one, the step or the question needs fixing, not the people.

Supervisor observation. Does the person do the task correctly at the station? This is the real test, and the sign-off stays with the supervisor.

Floor signals. Fewer repeated questions about the same task, fewer redone jobs, fewer notes in handover about the same mistake. Track these in your own operation rather than relying on outside benchmarks.

Keep all of this in one place so you can see who is ready for which station. Our employee training tracker guide shows a simple way to set it up.

## Common microlearning mistakes

Most microlearning fails because the lessons are not really micro, not tied to a real task, or never checked on the floor.

Cutting a long course into short clips. Ten short pieces of a lecture are still a lecture. Build each lesson around one task.

Lessons nobody can find at the station. If people cannot open the lesson on a phone when they need it, it will not be used.

Using micro lessons to skip the welcome. New hires still need a person, a tour and a team.

Treating a finished lesson as a trained person. A quiz shows understanding. Doing the task correctly under supervision is the sign-off.

Assigning everything to everyone. A long list of irrelevant lessons teaches people to click through.

No owner and no updates. A lesson that shows the old setting is worse than no lesson.

Trivia quizzes. Ask about decisions and checks, not the color of a bucket.

## Doing this with Flexlore

Flexlore is built around this kind of micro lesson. You film one job on a phone, mark the steps in the editor, and Flexlore drafts the step text and a short AI quiz. Your team edits and approves every draft before it is published. You assign lessons by role and location, and see who watched each one and passed its quiz, by person, team and location. Your team watches on iOS or Android, and the app is available in 8 languages.

## Questions

**What is an example of microlearning?**
A short video showing a line cook how to close the fryer station, cut into a few steps with a line of text each, followed by three quiz questions. Other examples are a machine changeover on a packaging line or a hotel room turndown. Each lesson covers one task from start to finish and can be watched on a phone.

**How long should a microlearning lesson be?**
As long as one task takes to show, and no longer. Most lessons for shift workers can be watched in a few minutes. If a lesson keeps growing, it usually covers two or three tasks and should be split. What matters more than length is that each step shows one action with one result.

**Can microlearning replace classroom training?**
Not fully. Microlearning works well for single tasks, refreshers and teams on different shifts. Classroom or face-to-face time is still better for welcome and culture, group practice, and complex topics that need discussion. Most frontline teams get the best result from a blend of both, with supervised practice on the floor.

**Is microlearning effective for frontline workers?**
It suits frontline work because lessons are short, tied to one task and can be watched on a phone around shift schedules. Whether it works in your operation is something to check yourself: look at completion, which quiz questions people miss, and whether supervisors see the task done correctly on the floor.

**How do I create microlearning content without a training team?**
Start with the tasks new hires ask about most. Film the person who does each task best on a phone, one task per video, cut it into a few steps, write a line of text for each and add three to five quiz questions. Have the expert check it and the manager approve it.

**How often should employees repeat micro lessons?**
Repeat a lesson a few times with growing gaps between, rather than many times at once. Refresh rare tasks before people need them, and resend a lesson whenever the task changes. Watching the steps again right before doing a task that has not been done for a while is often the most useful refresher.

**What is the difference between microlearning and an LMS?**
Microlearning is a way of designing training: short lessons, one task each. An LMS is a type of software for managing courses, often built around longer desk-based modules. Short task lessons can live in many tools. What matters for shift teams is that people can open them on a phone at the station.

# On-the-job training: how to structure it so every new hire learns the same job
URL: https://www.flexlore.com/guides/on-the-job-training/
Language: en

On-the-job training is training done at the real workstation, during real work, with an experienced person teaching the job. Structured on-the-job training follows a written plan: the trainer shows each task, the new hire does it with support, then alone while watched, and a supervisor signs it off.

## What is on-the-job training?

On-the-job training (OJT) is training that happens at the real workstation, during real work, with an experienced person teaching the job step by step. The new hire learns on the actual fryer, line or cart, not in a classroom.
For frontline work, most of the job is learned this way anyway. A cook learns the grill on the grill. An operator learns a changeover on the machine. The question is not whether to do on-the-job training, but whether it is planned or left to chance.
Unplanned OJT usually sounds like "stand next to Sam and watch." Planned OJT has a named trainer, a list of tasks for the station, a set order, a check of understanding and a dated sign-off. Both happen on the floor. Only one gives every new hire the same job.

## Job shadowing vs structured on-the-job training

Job shadowing means the new hire watches an experienced worker do the job. Structured OJT adds a plan, practice under supervision and a check at the end. Shadowing is one step inside structured OJT, not a replacement for it.
 | Job shadowing | Structured OJT | 
What the new hire does | Mostly watches and helps | Watches, does the task with support, then does it alone | 
Plan | Usually none; follows whatever the shift brings | A written task list and order for the station | 
Trainer | Whoever is on shift | A named, prepared trainer | 
What gets taught | That person's version of the job | The agreed standard for the job | 
Check at the end | Rarely | Questions on the steps and a supervisor sign-off | 
Record | Memory | Date, trainer and sign-off per task | 
Best for | Seeing the pace of a shift, meeting the team, getting a feel for a role | Learning a station well enough to work it alone | 
Shadowing has real uses. A day watching a busy service shows a new hire the rhythm of the job in a way no checklist can. It is also a good way to let someone try a role before moving into it. It just should not be the whole program, because what gets learned depends on who happened to be on shift.

## How to run on-the-job training: show, do together, do alone, check

Run each task through the same four steps: the trainer shows it, the new hire does it with the trainer beside them, the new hire does it alone while the trainer watches, and then the task is checked and signed off.
Show. The trainer does the task at normal speed once, then slowly, saying each step and why it matters ("basket out before the timer, or the oil drips onto the board"). Point out the one or two places where people usually go wrong.
Do together. The new hire does the task while the trainer stands beside them and talks them through it. The trainer corrects on the spot, but does not take over the task.
Do alone, watched. The new hire does the task without prompts, on a real shift, with the trainer nearby. Ask them to say the key steps out loud. If they skip a step, go back to step 2 for that task only.
Check and sign off. A few questions on the steps confirm they understood. A supervisor watches them do it on a normal shift and signs it off with a date.
Keep each pass to one task. "Learn the grill" is too big. "Light and season the grill at opening" is a task you can show, practice and check in one shift. Before you start, make sure the task has a written or filmed standard; a work instruction template is a quick way to write one.

## On-the-job training plan template: one station example

An OJT plan lists the tasks for one station in the order they should be learned, with the trainer, the target day and the sign-off for each. Here is a filled example for a new line cook on the fry station. Copy the structure and replace the tasks with your own.
Order | Task | Trainer | Target | Check | Signed off (supervisor, date) | 
1 | Station safety: hot oil, burns, where the fire blanket and extinguisher are | Fry lead | Day 1 | Questions |  | 
2 | Opening: switch on, oil level and quality check | Fry lead | Day 2 | Questions + watched |  | 
3 | Basket loading and cook times for each item | Fry lead | Day 2 to 3 | Questions + watched |  | 
4 | Holding times and when to throw product away | Fry lead | Day 3 | Questions |  | 
5 | Allergen orders on the fry station: separate fryer or procedure | Kitchen manager | Day 3 | Questions + watched |  | 
6 | Running the station on a busy shift with the trainer nearby | Fry lead | Day 4 to 6 | Watched |  | 
7 | Oil filtering and changing | Fry lead | Day 5 | Questions + watched |  | 
8 | Closing: shutdown, cleaning, end-of-shift checks | Fry lead | Day 6 | Watched |  | 
9 | Station sign-off: full shift alone, supervisor watching | Supervisor | Day 7 to 10 | Sign-off |  | 
The same shape works on a production line (start-up, quality checks, changeover, stoppages, shutdown) or in housekeeping (cart set-up, room order, bathroom, bed, final check). Keep the plan on one page and record the result in your training matrix, so the next shift lead can see who can work which station.

## How to choose and prepare the trainer

Pick someone who does the job to standard and can explain it patiently. The fastest worker on the line is not always that person.
Your best worker often does the job by feel. They skip steps in their head, use shortcuts that work for them, and get impatient with someone slow. That does not make them a bad trainer, but it means they need a little preparation. Look for:
Does it the standard way. If their version differs from the written one, agree which is right before they teach it.
Can say why. "Because the oil drips" sticks better than "just do it like this."
Lets people make small mistakes. Takes over only when safety or a customer is at risk.
Has the time. Training a new hire on the Saturday rush while running the station alone does not work. Plan the shifts.
Train the trainer briefly: walk them through the four-step method, the station plan and how sign-off works. Agree that they teach the written standard, not their personal variation. A skills matrix also shows who is able to train others on each station, which helps when cross-training staff across shifts.

## How to capture an expert's know-how before they leave

Film the expert doing the job once, split the video into steps, write a short note for each step and add a few questions. Then their method survives a holiday, a shift change or a resignation.
In many teams the real standard lives in one person: the operator who knows the sound of a bad changeover, the baker who knows when the dough is ready. When they leave, the next person learns a weaker copy from someone who watched them once.
Film them at the real station, on a phone, at normal working speed. No script.
Ask them to say out loud what they check and why, especially the small signals.
Split the video into short steps, one action each, so a learner can replay only the step they need.
Write a line or two under each step, with the key value or warning.
Add three to five questions about what goes wrong in real life.
Have the expert and a supervisor approve the result before it is used.
The video does not replace the trainer. It makes the "show" step the same for everyone, and gives the new hire something to come back to on day 4 when they forget. This is the core of master to apprentice skills transfer.

## How to check understanding and sign off OJT

Use two checks: questions to confirm the new hire understood the steps, and a supervisor watching them do the job on a real shift. Only the second one is a sign-off.
Questions should match the floor: "What do you do if the oil is below the line?", "Which check comes before you restart after a changeover?" Short and specific beats long and general. Questions show understanding; they do not prove the person can do it with a queue building.
The sign-off does that. A supervisor, not the trainer alone, watches the full task, confirms it is done to the standard and records the date. Until then, the person works the task with support. For safety-related tasks (machines, chemicals, lifting, hot oil), local rules decide what training and records are required, so check them and add those items to the plan. Keep sign-offs in one place, for example an employee training tracker, so nobody relies on memory.

## How to keep on-the-job training the same across locations

Use one task list, one filmed standard per task and one sign-off rule for every site, and compare progress by location.
Head office or the central team owns the shared task list and the standard for each task.
Each location names its own trainers but teaches the shared version. Local additions (a different oven, a different line) are added, not swapped in.
Every new hire watches the same filmed "show" step before the trainer works with them.
Area managers look at sign-offs by location to see which site is behind or where one trainer is carrying everything.

## Common on-the-job training mistakes

Shadowing only. Watching for a week without doing, checking or signing off.
The busiest shift as the classroom. Nobody has time to explain during a rush. Start on a quieter shift.
Whoever is free trains. Every shift teaches a slightly different job.
Too much at once. A whole station on day one. Go task by task.
The trainer signs off their own trainee. Keep the sign-off with a supervisor.
No record. Six months later nobody knows who was trained on what.
The expert's method is never written down. When they leave, it leaves with them.

## Doing this with Flexlore

Flexlore covers the "show" step and the record. Your expert films a task on a phone at the station and marks the steps in the phone editor. AI drafts the written steps and a short quiz, and your team reviews and approves them before anything goes out.
You assign tasks by role and location. New hires watch on their own phone, replay any step and take the quiz. You see who watched each task and passed its quiz, by person, team and location. Signing someone off on the floor stays with their supervisor. Plans are by number of users, see pricing.

## Questions

**What is the difference between job shadowing and on-the-job training?**
Job shadowing means watching an experienced worker do the job. On-the-job training includes shadowing but adds a plan, practice with support, doing the task alone while being watched, and a check at the end. Shadowing helps a new hire see the pace of a role; structured OJT is how they learn to work a station alone.

**How long should on-the-job training take?**
It depends on the station, not a fixed number of days. Plan it task by task: simple tasks can be signed off in a shift, complex stations take longer. Write a target day for each task in the plan, and treat the station as done only when a supervisor has signed off every task.

**What should an on-the-job training plan include?**
List the tasks for one station in learning order, and for each one name the trainer, set a target day, say how it will be checked (questions, watched, or both) and leave space for the supervisor's sign-off with a date. Keep it to one page per station.

**Who should do on-the-job training?**
A named trainer who does the job to the agreed standard and can explain why each step matters. The best performer is not always the best trainer. Give the trainer the station plan and the method, plan their shifts so they have time, and keep the final sign-off with a supervisor.

**How do you train the trainer for frontline staff?**
Keep it short and practical. Walk the trainer through the show, do together, do alone, check method, agree that they teach the written standard rather than their own shortcuts, show them the station plan and explain who signs off. Then watch them train one task and give feedback.

**Can video replace on-the-job training?**
No, but it improves it. A filmed standard makes the show step the same for every new hire and gives them something to replay later. The new hire still needs to practise the task on the real station with a trainer and be signed off by a supervisor.

**Is on-the-job training enough for safety training?**
It is often where safety is taught in practice, but local rules decide what safety training, certificates and records are required for each role. Check the rules that apply to your location and add those items to the plan, with their own sign-off.
